ECE 6390

Rebuilding a signal from its samples

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows samples of a cosine, three of the sinc pulses they scale, and the sum that rebuilds the continuous signal.

Uniform sampling records x[n] = x(nT) at interval T = 1/fₛ. If the original signal is band-limited below fₛ/2, the samples determine it completely, and the ideal reconstruction is x(t) = Σₙ x[n]·sinc((t − nT)/T), with sinc(v) = sin(πv)/(πv).

Each sinc pulse equals one at its own sample time and zero at every other sample time, so the sum passes exactly through the samples. Between samples many neighbouring pulses contribute. Their tails decay slowly, as 1/t, so a finite sum leaves a truncation error that shrinks as more terms are included.

In frequency, the sinc pulse is an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff fₛ/2: reconstruction keeps the baseband copy of the sampled spectrum and rejects the copies at multiples of fₛ. A signal above fₛ/2 produces the same samples as its alias below fₛ/2, so the reconstruction returns the alias. That is why the anti-alias filter belongs before the sampler.

Practical converters replace the ideal sinc with a realizable filter that needs a transition band, which is why real systems sample somewhat faster than twice the highest signal frequency.

Example

A cosine at 0.18 cycles per sample is rebuilt by 25 sinc terms to within about 0.017 over the eight sample intervals around t = 0. A cosine at 0.7 cycles per sample gives exactly the same samples as one at 0.3 cycles per sample, so the sinc sum rebuilds the 0.3 cycle-per-sample cosine.

Practice

1. Why does the reconstruction equal x[m] exactly at t = mT no matter how many terms are summed?

Evaluate sinc((mT − nT)/T) for integers m and n.

sinc(m − n) is one when n = m and zero for every other integer, so only the term n = m contributes at t = mT, and it contributes exactly x[m].

2. A 9 kHz tone is sampled at 12 kHz without an anti-alias filter. What frequency does ideal reconstruction produce?

Fold the frequency into the band from 0 to fₛ/2.

12 − 9 = 3 kHz. The samples of the 9 kHz tone match those of a 3 kHz tone, and reconstruction returns the 3 kHz tone.
